objective: By the end of this lesson you can brief passengers to the rules, use checklists, check that your navigation data is current, secure everything in the cabin, and manage automation, inoperative equipment and passenger distractions using SRM.
why: Most accidents trace back to a pilot error, not the airplane. An organized flight deck, a good briefing and disciplined checklist use remove many of those errors before the engine even starts.

prereading.what: Risk and resource management, SRM, ground operations with passengers and baggage, engine start safety.

prereading.label: PHAK 2-14 to 2-16

warmup: Your passenger asks to bring a camera bag, a cooler and a tablet. Where does each one go, and what do you tell them before you start the engine?

key_terms.def: The pilot directly responsible for, and the final authority on, the operation of the aircraft (14 CFR 91.3).
What the PIC tells everyone aboard before flight: belts, harnesses, doors, exits, emergency gear, conduct.
No talk or actions unrelated to flying during busy phases like taxi, takeoff and landing.
A memory aid so critical items are not missed. Use it for every phase of flight.
The stored airports, waypoints and airspace in a GPS or EFB. It has an expiration date.
Electronic flight bag: a tablet or display that shows charts, checklists, POH and more.
Portable electronic device: phones, tablets, laptops and similar consumer devices.
Minimum equipment list: an FAA-approved list for one aircraft that allows flight with certain items inoperative.
Single-pilot resource management: managing all resources inside and outside the airplane to fly safely alone.
Display that shows which autopilot modes are engaged and which are armed (in the RMH example, engaged = green, armed = white; colors vary by system).
Standard operating procedure: a written, tested procedure applied the same way every time, for normal, abnormal and emergency operations.
The pilot who watches the airplane's state and systems, calls out deviations from the intended flight path, and steps in if needed. The other pilot is the pilot flying (PF).

chunks.title: The passenger briefing: what the rules say

body.p: You are the PIC. You are directly responsible for, and the final authority on, the operation of the aircraft [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]]. Say so in your briefing, so nobody wonders who makes the calls.

head: Rule
What the PIC must do
rows: Before takeoff, make sure each person is briefed on how to fasten and unfasten their safety belt and, if installed, shoulder harness [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]].
Before moving on the surface, takeoff, or landing, make sure each person has been told to fasten their belt and, if installed, harness [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(2)]].
Each person must be in an approved seat with belt (and harness, if installed) secured during movement on the surface, takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]].
A person who has not reached their second birthday may be held by an adult in an approved seat [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(i)]].
Stay at your station with your belt fastened for takeoff, landing and en route; shoulder harness fastened for takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.105]].

body.p: A car seat may be used only if it carries the right labels and is secured to an approved forward-facing seat [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)]]. Booster seats, vest- or harness-type child restraints and lap-held child restraints are not approved for aircraft, unless the device itself was approved by the FAA (for example, by TSO-C100b or later) [[60:442|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(iii)(B)(4)]].
The FAA says a good briefing also tells passengers how you will keep distractions down in the cockpit, and should include the 91.107(a)(1) and (2) items [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.3.1]].

callout.text: 91.107 has three parts: BRIEF how belts work (before takeoff), NOTIFY to fasten (before taxi, takeoff, landing), and everyone must be SEATED and BELTED (taxi, takeoff, landing).

check.q: Before which three events must the PIC make sure each person was told to fasten their belt?
check.a: Moving on the surface, takeoff, and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(2)]].

body.p: The PHAK gives an easy memory aid for the briefing: SAFETY [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

head: Letter
Cover this
rows: Seat belts fastened for taxi, takeoff, landing. Shoulder harness fastened for takeoff, landing. Seat position adjusted and locked [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].
Air vents, all environmental controls, and what to do if a passenger feels sick [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].
Fire extinguisher: where it is and how to use it [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].
Exit doors (how to secure and open), emergency evacuation plan, emergency/survival kit [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].
Traffic: scan, spot and tell the pilot. Talking: sterile flight deck expectations [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

body.p: The ACS also wants these items. Add them to SAFETY:

bullets: Who is PIC. In training, brief the three-step control exchange: "You have the flight controls" / "I have the flight controls" / "You have the flight controls" [[24:37|AFH 1-16]].

Propeller. Passengers should move on the ramp only as you direct, or with an escort [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. A spinning propeller can be lethal if it strikes someone [[24:53|AFH 2-16]]. Before start you clear the area and call "CLEAR" [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
Doors. Show how to latch them. If one pops open in flight, it seldom affects the airplane's ability to fly; nobody unbuckles to reach it, and you will land normally [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].
Conduct and sterile flight deck. No talking to the pilot from departure until clear of the local airspace, and again during arrival [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].
Other items: smoking, route, altitudes, time en route, weather, and what the controls do [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

callout.text: SAFETY + P-P-D: Pilot in command, Propeller, Doors.

check.q: What does the "T" in SAFETY stand for?
check.a: Traffic (scan, spot, tell the pilot) and Talking (sterile flight deck expectations) [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

chunks.title: Use the right checklist, every time

body.p: A checklist is a memory aid. It helps make sure critical items are not missed. It does not have to be a "do list": you can do the items, then use the checklist to check they are done [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]. Pilots who stop taking checklists seriously start relying on memory, and the odds turn toward error [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].
At a minimum, use checklists for these phases [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]:

bullets: Preflight inspection
Before engine start
Engine starting
Before taxiing
Before takeoff
After takeoff
Cruise
Descent
Before landing
After landing
Engine shutdown and securing

body.p: Flying solo? Read the checklist out loud and touch each critical switch or control. Speaking and touching make it more likely the item really got done [[1:62|PHAK 2-23]]. A passenger can also read items or confirm one after you [[1:62|PHAK 2-23]]. The POH must be on board and is key for planning and equipment problems [[1:62|PHAK 2-23]].

AC 120-71B, the FAA's guide to standard operating procedures (SOPs), adds: in single-pilot airplanes, keep the Before-Takeoff and Before-Landing checklists on the panel and touch each control to verify its position [[59:19|AC 120-71B 5.2.1]]. Its checklist tips [[59:22|AC 120-71B 5.6.4]]:

bullets: Remember to use the checklist.
Check every item, every time.
Slow down and confirm significant items.
Deliberately read the checklist.
If interrupted, restart from the beginning.

body.p: Avoid doing a checklist while taxiing: you cannot pay full attention to both [[59:17|AC 120-71B 5.1.3]] [[59:18|AC 120-71B 5.1.3]]. Start each checklist at a clear, set point (for example, a set spot before the hold-short line) so it is not forgotten or rushed [[59:18|AC 120-71B 5.1.5]].
Finish all pre-taxi checklist items before you taxi [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.3.2]].

callout.text: Use the checklist from your airplane's POH/AFM. Checklists differ by airplane.

check.q: Name two ways a solo pilot can make checklist use more reliable.
check.a: Read it out loud and touch each critical control as you check it [[1:62|PHAK 2-23]].

body.p: Your GPS, panel display or EFB holds a database of airports, waypoints and airspace. It expires. The PHAK counts database currency as part of the "Plane" in the 5 Ps, and publications currency as part of the "Plan" [[1:53|PHAK 2-14]].

head: Use
Requirement
rows: Onboard navigation data must be current and appropriate for the region [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]]. Before use, check the database date and make sure your flight is before its expiration [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]].

Databases should be updated, but there is no requirement for VFR navigation [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]]. Don't use a moving map with an outdated database in and around critical airspace [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]].
Navigation or performance information must be current, up to date and valid, as verified by the pilot [[42:3|AC 91-78A 9.1]].

body.p: If your database is expired and you can't update it, ignore the moving map's airspace for critical decisions. Waypoints may be gone or moved; check them against a current Chart Supplement or sectional [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]].

VFR GPS receivers have no RAIM alerting, so cross-check position with pilotage or other navigation [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]]. Do not rely only on GPS for VFR navigation [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17]]. The moving map never replaces a VFR sectional [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]].

callout.text: Enter your route and waypoints on the ground, not in the air [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]]. Verify the route against a current chart.

check.q: Is an expired GPS database legal for VFR? Is it smart near Class B?
check.a: There is no requirement to update for VFR, but the AIM says not to use an outdated moving map in and around critical airspace; verify waypoints with current charts [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]].

body.p: Loose items can jam controls, block your view, hit someone in turbulence, or move the CG.

bullets: Baggage: supervise loading yourself. Unsecured or badly loaded baggage can change the CG [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

Real accidents: hunters' dogs, not secured, ran aft on takeoff; the CG went past the aft limit and the airplane stalled and crashed. Unsecured skydivers sitting aft caused the same result [[22:20|W&B Handbook 1-6]].
Under the pedals: an instructor found a student's water bottle under a rudder pedal after a solo flight [[25:42|AIH 2-9]].
Glare shield: maps and other cockpit objects must be removed and stowed during flight so they don't block your view [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Turbulence: in moderate turbulence unsecured objects are dislodged; in severe, they are tossed about [[34:106|AIM TBL 7-1-11]].
Tablets and EFBs: plan where they are stowed for takeoff and landing; an unsecured EFB is a hazard [[42:4|AC 91-78A 11.1]].

callout.text: Before engine start, do a "cabin sweep": bags tied down or belted, nothing on the floor near the pedals, nothing on the glare shield, tablet in its mount or stowed, empty seats' belts fastened.
Baggage weight limits, tie-down points and placards are POH-specific. Check them for your airplane.

check.q: Why can an unsecured bag in the back be more than a nuisance?
check.a: It can shift aft and move the CG; unsecured loads moving aft on takeoff have caused stall accidents [[22:20|W&B Handbook 1-6]] [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

body.p: Automation can cut workload and boost awareness [[30:50|RMH 7-1]]. It can also add work, confuse you, or make you complacent [[30:51|RMH 7-2]]. Use it to manage workload, not to cover a lack of skill [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

bullets: Anticipate: know what should happen before you push a button or turn a knob [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].
Act: push the buttons and turn the knobs [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].
Verify: make sure the airplane or avionics does what you expected [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

body.p: Know at all times which modes are engaged and which are armed, and verify armed modes engage when they should [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. Changing the navigation source can drop the autopilot to wings-level mode [[30:52|RMH 7-3]].

bullets: Program and check routes on the ground; compare with a paper log or chart [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].
If automation isn't doing what you expect, reduce the level of automation or fly by hand [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].
A common error is not stepping down to a lower level of automation when things change [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].
Know how to disconnect the autopilot and where its checklists are [[30:53|RMH 7-4]].
Stop, look and read before pushing buttons [[1:69|PHAK 2-30]].

body.p: Portable devices (PEDs). 14 CFR 91.21 bans PEDs on air carrier aircraft and on any aircraft operated under IFR, except voice recorders, hearing aids, pacemakers, shavers, and devices the operator has determined won't interfere with navigation or communication. On aircraft not run by an air carrier, the PIC (or other operator) makes that call [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21]]. The FAA treats the PIC or renter-pilot as the "operator" [[43:2|AC 91.21-1D 6.1]]. If a device causes interference, turn it off [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 7.2.3]]. Tell passengers your PED rules in the briefing [[43:5|AC 91.21-1D 8.2]].

check.q: Annunciator shows HDG and ALT in green, LOC and GS in white. What is the autopilot doing?
check.a: Holding heading and altitude; approach (LOC/GS) is armed but not engaged [[30:52|RMH 7-3]].

body.p: All installed instruments and equipment are required to work before each departure, unless you legally defer the item [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. If you find something broken before flight: cancel, get it fixed, or defer it [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].
Most small piston airplanes have no MEL, so use 14 CFR 91.213(d). The item may NOT be [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]]:

bullets: Part of the VFR-day type certification instruments and equipment
Required on the aircraft's equipment list or Kinds of Operations Equipment List
Required by 91.205 or another rule for this kind of flight
Required by an airworthiness directive

body.p: If it passes all four: remove it (placard and log it) or deactivate it and placard it "Inoperative" [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)]]. A rated pilot or mechanic must decide it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(4)]]. If deactivation needs maintenance, a mechanic does it and logs it [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

If an aircraft has an approved MEL and Letter of Authorization, you must use the MEL [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. Deferrals are not for things that break in flight; use the POH procedures then [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

callout.text: Think beyond legal. An inoperative autopilot may be legal, yet turn a night approach into an unfamiliar airport from medium to serious risk [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]]. Several inop items together deserve extra thought [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

check.q: Day VFR, no MEL, position lights inoperative. What do you do?
check.a: Follow 91.213(d): if not required for this flight, deactivate (e.g., pull the breaker), placard INOPERATIVE, and determine it's not a hazard [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].

body.p: Many accidents start with a distraction that pulls your eyes from the instruments or the window [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. A chatty passenger in the pattern is exactly that.

Your capacity is limited. When the task load is bigger than your capacity, tasks get done badly or not at all [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]]. Plan ahead: set radios and charts early and finish checklists well in advance [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. If overloaded: stop, think, slow down, prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

bullets: Brief the sterile flight deck before engine start. Avoid all non-flight talk during taxi, takeoff and landing; no extra conversation or cell phone use [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.3.5]].
Set up NAV/COM before taxi. Setting radios while rolling is the leading cause of "heads down" [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.3.3]].
Keep passengers informed when workload is low [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].
Turn the passenger into help: watch for traffic, read checklist items, hold the chart [[1:62|PHAK 2-23]] [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].
If a door pops open: fly the airplane first. Open-door accidents come from distraction, not the door [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

callout.text: Aviate first. A problem in the cabin is never more important than flying the airplane.

check.q: Your passenger starts asking about a landmark on short final. What do you do, and what should you have done earlier?
check.a: Politely say "not now" and keep flying. Earlier: brief the sterile flight deck for takeoff and landing [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.3.5]] [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

chunks.title: ADM and SRM on every flight

body.p: About 85 percent of aviation accidents are caused by "failure of the pilot to..." [[24:49|AFH 2-12]]. SRM means managing all resources, inside and outside the airplane, to make the flight succeed [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]]. It joins situational awareness, human resource management, task management and ADM [[24:50|AFH 2-13]].

head: Tool
What it is
rows: Review the Plan, Plane, Pilot, Passengers and Programming at least five times before and during flight [[1:54|PHAK 2-15]]. On flights over 2 hours, do it hourly [[1:53|PHAK 2-14]].
Perceive hazards (PAVE), Process risk (CARE), Perform risk controls (TEAM) [[1:54|PHAK 2-15]].

body.p: Resources: ATC and flight service outside; the passenger, checklists, POH and your own knowledge inside [[1:62|PHAK 2-23]]. Plan in advance when and where you will program the avionics, and when you won't [[1:54|PHAK 2-15]].

Passengers may not see risk the way you do. Give them the facts and involve them in the decision; this removes self-made pressure [[1:54|PHAK 2-15]]. Never let anyone else make risk decisions for you [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]].

SOPs and pilot monitoring. An SOP is a written, tested procedure used the same way every time [[59:7|AC 120-71B 1.4]]. When two pilots fly (you and your instructor, or a safety pilot), one is the pilot flying (PF), who controls the flight path, and one is the pilot monitoring (PM), who watches the airplane's state, calls out deviations and steps in if needed [[59:7|AC 120-71B 1.4]] [[59:24|AC 120-71B 6.4]]. Hand over roles out loud: a verbal handoff, a verbal acceptance and a short brief of the airplane's state [[59:24|AC 120-71B 6.4]].
Monitoring well means [[59:23|AC 120-71B 6.2]]:

bullets: Following SOPs every time
Calling out deviations clearly
Managing distractions and staying alert
Speaking up if the autopilot modes or the airplane are not doing what you expected
Remembering that displays can be wrong; look for other evidence that confirms them

body.p: Watch for monitoring lapses under time pressure, high workload, and also when things are quiet and boredom or complacency sets in [[59:23|AC 120-71B 6.3.1]] [[59:24|AC 120-71B 6.3.6]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step, plus common errors

body.p: There is no single FAA flow for flight deck management. This order pulls the steps from the sources above. Use your POH checklists for the airplane-specific items.

bullets: 1. Before you get in: run the 5 Ps and PAVE [[1:54|PHAK 2-15]]. Check database dates and chart currency [[33:92|AIM 1-1-17]] [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]].
2. Check for inoperative items; apply 91.213(d) or the MEL [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].
3. Supervise loading; secure bags and loose items [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. Escort passengers on the ramp [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].
4. Organize the cockpit: charts, frequencies, materials, nothing on the glare shield [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
5. Brief passengers: PIC, SAFETY, propeller, doors, sterile flight deck, PEDs [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]] [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107]].
6. Before start checklist; clear the prop area, call "CLEAR" [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
7. Program avionics and autopilot on the ground; verify route and waypoints [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. Set up NAV/COM before taxi [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.3.3]].
8. Use checklists every phase; Anticipate-Act-Verify on every automation change [[24:36|AFH 1-15]] [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].
9. Keep re-running the 5 Ps in flight [[1:54|PHAK 2-15]].

head: ACS element
What the examiner wants to see
rows: Secure all items in the aircraft.

Conduct an appropriate passenger briefing, including identifying the pilot-in-command (PIC), use of safety belts, shoulder harnesses, doors, passenger conduct, sterile aircraft, propeller blade avoidance, and emergency procedures.
Properly program and manage the aircraft's automation, as applicable.
Appropriately manage risks by utilizing ADM, including SRM/CRM.

body.p: Common errors:

bullets: Flying from memory instead of the checklist [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].
Briefing belts but skipping doors, prop, PIC or sterile flight deck (ACS PA.II.B.S2).
Loose bottle, headset bag or tablet left on the floor or glare shield [[25:42|AIH 2-9]] [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Programming the GPS while taxiing or in the air [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.3.3]] [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17]].
Not knowing which autopilot modes are engaged vs armed [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].
Staying in a high level of automation when things change [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].
Trusting an expired moving map near busy airspace [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]].
Letting a passenger or open door pull attention away from flying [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

callout.text: This Task's Skills elements have no number tolerances. The examiner judges your briefing, your organization and your decisions.

check.q: When should you load your route and waypoints into the GPS?
check.a: On the ground before flight, then verify against a current chart [[1:421|PHAK 16-34]] [[33:91|AIM 1-1-17]].

scenario.title: Saturday trip with two friends
scenario.setup: You are taking two non-pilot friends on a 1-hour VFR flight to a busy airport under a Class B shelf. During preflight you find the autopilot placarded INOP and your tablet app says the GPS database expired last week. One friend brings a cooler and a camera bag and wants to film the landing from the right seat. The other is nervous and keeps asking questions.

questions.q: The autopilot is placarded INOP. Can you go, and does it change your risk?
questions.a: If it is not required for this flight under 91.213(d) and is properly placarded, it can be deferred [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]. But plan to hand-fly and reduce other workload; losing an autopilot can raise risk on a demanding flight [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]].

questions.q: Your tablet database is expired. What now?
questions.a: Update it if you can. If not, don't trust the moving map's airspace for critical decisions; verify waypoints and the Class B shelf with a current sectional or Chart Supplement [[1:420|PHAK 16-33]] [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]].

questions.q: Where do the cooler and camera bag go?
questions.a: Secured in the baggage area within the POH limits, loaded under your supervision so they can't shift or change the CG [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. Nothing loose near the pedals or on the glare shield [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

questions.q: How do you handle the filming friend and the nervous friend?
questions.a: Brief a sterile flight deck for taxi, takeoff and landing, and the camera stays secure then [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.3.5]]. Give the nervous friend a job, like spotting traffic, and keep them informed when workload is low [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

questions.q: Use the 5 Ps. Should you go?
questions.a: Review Plan, Plane, Pilot, Passengers, Programming [[1:54|PHAK 2-15]]. If the combined hazards (no autopilot, old database, busy airspace, distracting passengers) feel like too much, mitigate (new database, simpler route) or delay. Never let passengers make the risk decision for you [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]].

skills.do: Show the examiner that all baggage and loose items are secured, nothing is near the controls or on the glare shield, and your tablet or EFB is mounted or stowed.
skills.practice: Do a cabin sweep before every flight: floor, seats, back, glare shield, side pockets. Say it out loud.

skills.do: Brief the examiner as a passenger: PIC, belts and harnesses, doors, passenger conduct, sterile flight deck, propeller avoidance and emergency procedures.
skills.practice: Write your briefing on a card using SAFETY plus PIC, Propeller, Doors. Practice it on friends until it is smooth and short.

skills.do: If equipped, program the GPS and autopilot before taxi, verify the route, and call out modes engaged and armed in flight.
skills.practice: Use the avionics simulator or trainer app at home. Practice Anticipate-Act-Verify on each button push.

skills.do: Talk through your 5 Ps and PAVE. Explain how you would handle an inop item, an expired database, or a distracting passenger.
skills.practice: Before each lesson, write a quick PAVE list and one risk control for each hazard. Ask your CFI to throw in a surprise problem.

quiz.q: Under 14 CFR 91.107, before takeoff the PIC must make sure each person is briefed on:
options: The route and destination weather
The location of the ELT
The aircraft's weight and balance
How to fasten and unfasten their safety belt and, if installed, shoulder harness
quiz.why: 91.107(a)(1) requires the belt and harness fasten/unfasten briefing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(1)]].

quiz.q: Each person on board must be in a seat with belt fastened during:
options: Movement on the surface, takeoff and landing
Takeoff and landing only, since taxiing is not part of flight
All phases of flight
Only when the PIC says so
quiz.why: 91.107(a)(3) covers movement on the surface, takeoff and landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)]].

quiz.q: In the SAFETY briefing, "F" stands for:
options: Fuel selector
Flight controls, and keeping feet and hands clear of the yoke and pedals
Frequencies
Fire extinguisher location and operation

quiz.q: For VFR use of a GPS, the AIM says the database:
options: Must be updated every 28 days
Is never needed
Should be updated, but is not required to be; don't use an outdated moving map near critical airspace
Must be updated only for Class B
quiz.why: No requirement for VFR, but updating is recommended and an outdated moving map should not be used around critical airspace [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]].

quiz.q: Under 14 CFR 91.21, who may decide a PED won't interfere in a Part 91 airplane (not an air carrier)?
options: The pilot in command or other operator
The aircraft manufacturer, through its published list of approved devices
Only the FAA
Any passenger who owns the device and says it is safe to use
quiz.why: For aircraft other than certificate holders, the determination may be made by the PIC or other operator [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21(c)]].

quiz.q: On the autopilot annunciator, LOC and GS are shown in white. This means:
options: They are engaged and the autopilot is already flying the approach
They are armed but not engaged
They are failed
They are not installed
quiz.why: White LOC and GS mean approach mode is armed but not engaged [[30:52|RMH 7-3]].

quiz.q: Using 91.213(d), which inoperative item can NOT be deferred?
options: An item not on the equipment list
An installed item not required for this flight
One required by an airworthiness directive
A courtesy light
quiz.why: Items required by an AD can't be deferred under 91.213(d) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iv)]].

quiz.q: A cabin door pops open just after liftoff. Best action?
options: Unbuckle and close it
Turn back right away with a steep turn to put the airplane back on the runway quickly
Fly the airplane, fly a normal pattern, and land
Slow to stall speed
quiz.why: Concentrate on flying, don't rush, fly a normal pattern and landing, and leave the door alone [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

quiz.q: AC 120-71B says that if you are interrupted while running a checklist, you should:
options: Finish it from memory
Pick up at the item you think you were on
Skip to the last item and call it complete
Restart from the beginning
quiz.why: Its checklist error prevention tips include: if interrupted, restart from the beginning [[59:22|AC 120-71B 5.6.4]].

takeaways: You are PIC: brief belts, harnesses, doors, prop, conduct, sterile flight deck and emergencies before every flight.
91.107: brief belts before takeoff; everyone belted for taxi, takeoff and landing.
Use the checklist for every phase; read it aloud and touch the controls.
Check database and chart currency; verify waypoints with current charts.
Secure everything; nothing loose near the pedals or on the glare shield.
Automation: Anticipate, Act, Verify, and step down a level when things change.
cfi_notes: Have the student brief you as a passenger on every lesson until it is smooth; examiners often ask to be briefed exactly like a passenger.
Students often skip doors, the propeller and identifying the PIC. Those are named in ACS PA.II.B.S2.
Check the floor and glare shield after solo flights; the AIH water-bottle story is a good teaching moment [[25:42|AIH 2-9]].
Examiners like to ask about 91.213(d) with a real placard or a pretend inop item; tie it to the aircraft's equipment list and KOEL.
For TAA, ask the student to tell you which modes are engaged and armed after every button push [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].
Ask about tablet database dates during preflight; have them show the expiration date on the device.
gaps: No FAA source here gives a single numbered flight deck management procedure; the step list combines AFH, PHAK, AIM and AC 61-98E guidance.
Baggage weight limits, tie-down points, cargo nets, checklists, autopilot modes and equipment lists/KOEL are airplane-specific: use the POH/AFM and avionics supplements.
The handbooks give little specific guidance on how to tie down cargo in small airplanes beyond supervising loading and keeping it secured.
This Task's Skills elements have no numeric ACS tolerances.

AC 120-71B is written mainly for Part 121 and 135 air carriers (it encourages other operators and pilot schools to use it). Its single-pilot guidance is limited to 5.2.1; pilot flying/monitoring content applies here only to dual instruction or flying with a safety pilot.

activities.title: Match the SAFETY letters
activities.intro: Tap a letter, then what you cover for it in the briefing.

pairs.r: Seat belts, shoulder harness, seat adjusted and locked
Air vents, cabin controls, what to do if someone feels sick
Fire extinguisher: where it is and how to use it
Exit doors, evacuation plan, survival kit
Spot traffic and tell the pilot; quiet times in the cockpit

activities.title: Checklists from ramp to landing
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the checklists in the order you use them, then tap Check.

activities.title: Anticipate, Act or Verify?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Before pressing NAV, know the autopilot should turn to join the course
Expect that switching the nav source may drop the autopilot to wings level
Turn the heading bug to the new heading
Check the annunciator shows the mode you chose as engaged
Watch that the armed glideslope mode engages when it should
Confirm the airplane levels off at the altitude you set

cards.s: If something breaks in flight, you defer it under 91.213(d) and keep going.
cards.why: No. Deferrals are not used for things that break in flight. Use the AFM/POH procedures instead [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]].

cards.s: An item the Kinds of Operations Equipment List requires for your flight can be deferred under 91.213(d).
cards.why: No. Items shown as required on the equipment list or the Kinds of Operations Equipment List for that flight can't be deferred [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(ii)]].

cards.s: Deactivating an item can be as simple as pulling its circuit breaker.
cards.why: Yes. Deactivation may be as simple as putting a circuit breaker in the OFF position. Complex jobs need a mechanic [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

cards.s: Once the FAA issues an MEL and Letter of Authorization for an airplane, you must use the MEL.
cards.why: Yes. After the LOA is issued, using the MEL becomes mandatory for that airplane [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]].

cards.s: A deferred item must be placarded INOPERATIVE.
cards.why: Yes. In all cases the item must be placarded INOPERATIVE [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)]].

cards.s: If an inoperative item is legally deferred, it adds no risk to the flight.
cards.why: No. Legal is not the same as safe. A broken autopilot can turn a dark night approach into an unfamiliar airport from medium to serious risk [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]].

final_quiz.q: Your friend climbs in for a sightseeing flight. Under 14 CFR 91.107, by what point must you have told them to fasten their seat belt?
options: Before you move the airplane on the ground
Before you start the engine
Before you reach the runway hold-short line
Before you climb above pattern altitude
final_quiz.why: The PIC must make sure each person was told to fasten their belt before moving on the surface, takeoff or landing [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(2)]]. The rule is tied to moving the airplane, not to engine start.

final_quiz.q: A passenger wants to hold her 20-month-old son on her lap for the flight. Under 14 CFR 91.107, is that allowed?
options: Yes, but only if the child is under 1 year old.
No. Every child must ride in an approved car seat.
Yes. A child who has not reached the second birthday may be held by an adult in an approved seat.
No. The child must have a seat and belt of his own.
final_quiz.why: A person who has not reached their second birthday may be held by an adult sitting in an approved seat [[60:441|14 CFR 91.107(a)(3)(i)]].

final_quiz.q: You are briefing your passenger on the sterile flight deck. Under FAA guidance, when should they hold all non-flight talk?
options: Only while you start the engine
Only in cruise, while you navigate and talk to ATC
For the whole flight, from engine start to shutdown
During taxi, takeoff and departure, and again during arrival and landing
final_quiz.why: AC 61-98E says to avoid all non-flight talk during critical phases such as taxi, takeoff and landing [[15:17|AC 61-98E 2.3.6.3.5]]. The PHAK adds departure until clear of the local airspace, and the arrival. It also says to keep passengers informed when workload is low, so a silent flight is not the goal [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

final_quiz.q: On a dual lesson your instructor says, "You have the flight controls." What should happen next?
options: You say "I have the flight controls," and the instructor confirms, "You have the flight controls."
You take the yoke without saying anything
You say "Roger, I've got it," and the instructor lets go as soon as he sees your hands are on the controls
You wiggle the yoke so the instructor can feel you have it
final_quiz.why: The AFH recommends a three-step exchange: "You have the flight controls," "I have the flight controls," then "You have the flight controls" again, plus a visual check [[24:37|AFH 1-16]].

final_quiz.q: AC 120-71B warns against "floating" checklist starts. Which habit follows its advice for the before-takeoff checklist?
options: Start it whenever you have a free moment during taxi, so it fits around the radio calls and turns
Run it from memory to save time at a busy airport
Start it at a set point you pick ahead of time, such as a spot before the hold-short line
Start it only after the tower clears you for takeoff
final_quiz.why: Anchor each checklist to a clear cue, like reaching a set point before the hold-short line. Floating starts make it easy to rush the checklist or forget it [[59:18|AC 120-71B 5.1.5]].

final_quiz.q: You plan a VFR flight that passes near Class C airspace. Your tablet's navigation database expired two weeks ago, and you can't update it. What does the AIM say?
options: The flight is illegal until the database is updated, because VFR flight requires current navigation data on board
You may go VFR, but don't rely on the old moving map near that airspace; check waypoints with current charts
Follow the moving map as usual, since database dates matter only for IFR
Turn the tablet off, because GPS may not be used for VFR
final_quiz.why: There is no requirement to update the database for VFR, but the AIM says not to use an outdated moving map in and around critical airspace. Verify waypoints with current products like a sectional or Chart Supplement [[33:90|AIM 1-1-17]].

final_quiz.q: A passenger brings his large dog and wants it to ride loose in the back. Why do you insist it be secured?
options: It only matters if you expect turbulence
A loose dog weighs more than a secured one
A loose dog makes the airplane nose-heavy on takeoff, which raises the stall speed and lengthens the takeoff roll
On takeoff it could move aft and push the CG past the aft limit, which has caused stall crashes
final_quiz.why: In a real accident, unsecured dogs ran aft on takeoff, the CG went well past the aft limit, and the airplane stalled and crashed [[22:20|W&B Handbook 1-6]]. Unsecured loads can change the CG [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].

final_quiz.q: During your cabin check before engine start, which item is set up correctly?
options: A sectional chart resting on the glare shield
A tablet locked in its mount
A camera bag sitting loose on the empty back seat
A water bottle on the floor near the rudder pedals
final_quiz.why: Maps on the glare shield must be removed and stowed [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]]. A loose bottle can end up under a rudder pedal [[25:42|AIH 2-9]]. Plan where the EFB is stowed, because an unsecured one is a hazard [[42:4|AC 91-78A 11.1]].

final_quiz.q: Your autopilot is tracking a GPS course in NAV mode. You switch the navigation source to VOR. With some autopilots, what can happen?
options: Nothing; the autopilot picks up the VOR course on its own and keeps tracking it without any input
The autopilot climbs to the last altitude you set
NAV mode drops out and the autopilot holds wings level until you re-engage NAV
The autopilot turns back toward the last GPS waypoint
final_quiz.why: With some autopilots, changing the nav source makes NAV mode disengage, and the autopilot defaults to wings level (ROL) until you act [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]] [[30:52|RMH 7-3]].

final_quiz.q: You are on autopilot in NAV mode when ATC gives you an unexpected reroute. Reprogramming the GPS is getting confusing and your workload is climbing. What is the best move?
options: Keep working the GPS until the new route is loaded, and let the autopilot fly
Step down to a lower level of automation, like heading and altitude modes, or hand-fly while you sort it out
Turn off the autopilot and the GPS and fly by dead reckoning only
Ask your passenger to finish programming the GPS
final_quiz.why: If automation isn't doing what you expect, reduce the level of automation or fly by hand. Failing to move to a lower level when things change is one of the most common errors [[30:51|RMH 7-2]].

final_quiz.q: You fly IFR in your club's Piper (not an air carrier). Under 14 CFR 91.21, which device may a passenger use without you first deciding it won't interfere?
options: A laptop
A hearing aid
A cell phone in airplane mode
A tablet playing a movie
final_quiz.why: Under IFR, PEDs are banned except voice recorders, hearing aids, pacemakers, electric shavers, and devices the operator has decided won't interfere [[60:438|14 CFR 91.21]]. The laptop, tablet and phone need that decision.

final_quiz.q: You plan a day VFR flight in a small piston airplane with no MEL. The landing light is inoperative. Assume it isn't required by the type certification, the equipment list or KOEL, 91.205, or an AD. What else must happen before takeoff?
options: Remove or deactivate it, placard it INOPERATIVE, and have a rated pilot or mechanic decide it is not a hazard
Nothing. Since it isn't required, you can just go.
Get a special flight permit from the FSDO
Have a mechanic repair it, because all installed equipment must work
final_quiz.why: Under 91.213(d), the item must be removed or deactivated and placarded, and a rated pilot or mechanic must decide it is not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)-(4)]]. A landing light is required by 91.205 only at night for hire, so day VFR it can be deferred [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]].

final_quiz.q: Two friends need to reach a meeting. The weather is fine along most of the route, but low IFR is forecast at your destination. Which choice follows SRM?
options: Promise them you will get there, since they are counting on you and a firm promise keeps everyone calm
Explain the risk plainly and plan an out, like a rental car at a fuel stop short of the bad weather
Let the passengers decide whether the weather is good enough to continue
Say nothing so they don't worry, and decide in flight
final_quiz.why: The PHAK's 5 Ps example plans a rental car at a fuel stop so the pilot isn't pressured to continue [[1:53|PHAK 2-14]]. Give passengers the facts and involve them [[1:54|PHAK 2-15]], but never let them make risk decisions for you [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]].
